item.title: How HAX Lab works
item.content:
HAX Lab is one part of a loop. A course teaches web development on real HAX problems, student clubs bring their own passions, the lab gives a few students a full term on one project, faculty fund work that solves their own problems, and graduates come back as mentors. Each part feeds the next.

The loop

IST 256 at Penn State teaches modern front-end development, using HAX as the backdrop rather than the subject. Class projects often become HAX blocks. In one term, 36 students filed 24 UX findings and 18 were fixed before the term ended.

Student clubs bring what they care about. The cyber security club ran two long audits and helped fix 30 vulnerabilities. Members of the UX club applied their training to the editor.

One-term internships in Arts and Architecture. Each student owns one real project from start to release, with code review from the maintainers.

Faculty fund student work that solves their own problems, and HAX gains the capability. See Faculty and funding.

Students leave with shipped work, not just a grade. Some come back as teaching assistants and mentors for the next group. See Graduates.

A term in the lab

  • One project you own. You pick it with the team from real needs in the unified issue queue and see it through to a release.
  • Real review. Your pull requests are reviewed like anyone else's. Feedback is the point.
  • Open office hours, three times a week. They're open to anyone, and they now draw contributors who were never in the lab.
  • Public credit. With your permission, your work is posted on LinkedIn with you tagged, so employers see what you shipped.

Ways in

Onboarding takes you from nothing to a pull request. It's the same path the class follows.

Come to office hours, or comment on an issue you want to try. Clubs are welcome to bring a group.

Contact Product Owner Bill Rose or Project Lead Bryan Ollendyke. Bring a link to something you've built.
